
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}{{Short description|Australian biologist and author}}
'''Tim Low''' {{Post-nominals|country=AUS|AM}} (born 1956), is an [[Australia|Australian]] [[biologist]] and author of books and articles on nature and [[conservation ethic|conservation]]. 

== Early life ==
Low became interested in [[reptile]]s as a teenager, regularly visiting the Queensland Museum after school to study the lizard collections under the guidance of then-curator [[Jeanette Covacevich]]. He contributed to the discovery of several new lizard species, collected on travels around Queensland. He described the [[Gehyra|chain-backed dtella]] (''Gehyra catenata'') and had the [[Menetia|dwarf litter-skink]] (''Menetia timlowi'') named after him.<ref> Low, Tim (1979) A new species of gecko, genus Gehyra (Reptilia: Gekkonidae) from Queensland. Victorian Naturalist (1979) 96: 190-196.</ref> It was later renamed ''[[Pygmaeascincus|Pygmaeascincus timlowi]]''.<ref>Beolens, Bo; Watkins, Michael; Grayson, Michael (2011). ''The Eponym Dictionary of Reptiles''. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press. xiii + 296 pp. {{ISBN|978-1-4214-0135-5}}. ("Low, T.", p. 161).</ref>

== Career ==
Low worked part-time at the Queensland Museum as an interpretation officer before developing a career as an independent environmental consultant and writer. For twenty years, he wrote a column in ''Nature Australia'' magazine.<ref>https://museum-publications.australian.museum/ </ref> For two years (2013–2015), Low was co-editor of ''Wildlife Australia'' magazine. For two years, he wrote the Wild Journey blog for ''Australian Geographic'' and contributed many articles to the magazine. He co-authored a 2023 report that reviewed the causes of Australia's modern extinctions.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2023-11-08 |title=Since 1960, Australia has lost 23 native animals in an extinction wave |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/rural/2023-11-08/native-species-lost-to-modern-extinction/103055638 |access-date=2023-11-08 |work=ABC News |language=en-AU}}</ref> 
 
His report, ''Climate Change and Queensland Biodiversity'', was announced in [[Parliament of Queensland|Queensland parliament]] by environment minister [[Kate Jones (politician)|Kate Jones]] in June 2011.<ref> Record of Proceedings, Queensland parliament, 14 June 2011, page 1764, from a Ministerial statement by the member for Ashgrove, Hon. Kate Jones.</ref> In that year, Low traveled to [[Europe]] and [[Alaska]] to study [[climate change]] under the [[Winston Churchill Memorial Trusts|Churchill Fellowship]]. Low also ran a workshop in [[Canberra]], writing up a report titled ''Climate Change and Invasive Species''. He has written journal articles that caution about the weed threats posed by [[Energy crop|biofuel crops]], [[Agroforestry|agroforestry trees]], and [[Pasture|pasture plants]].

Low lives in [[Brisbane]]. He was appointed a [[Order of Australia|Member of the Order of Australia]] in the [[2024 King's Birthday Honours (Australia)|2024 King's Birthday Honours]] for "significant service to conservation, and environmental education and awareness".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mr Tim Low |url=https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/3026520 |access-date=2024-06-10 |website=Australian Honours Search Facility}}</ref>

== Publications ==
His seventh book, ''Where Song Began: Australia's Birds and How They Changed the World'', tells the story of [[Australia]] as a land of aggressive birds that gave the world its songbirds and [[Parrot|parrots]]. Published in Australia by Penguin and internationally by [[Yale University Press]], it won the [[Australian Book Industry Awards]] prize for best General Non-Fiction in 2015 and People's Choice at the Victorian Premier's Literary Awards. It was also shortlisted for the [[New South Wales Premier's History Awards|NSW Premier's History Awards]].<ref>{{Cite magazine|date=Summer 2015|title=New South Wales Premier's Awards|url=https://www.sl.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/sl_magazine_summer_201516_web.pdf|magazine=SL Magazine|volume=8 |number=4|page=36}}</ref>

''The New Nature: Winners and Losers in Wild Australia'' (2002) explains that some native species benefit from human impacts, sometimes going on to cause environmental problems. It won the inaugural [[Nib Literary Award|Waverley Library Award for Literature]], now called the Nib Literary Award, and received a special mention at the Centre for Australian Cultural Studies National Awards. Because of this book, Low was invited to serve on the advisory committee (Biological Diversity Advisory Committee) of then-environment minister, Senator [[Ian Campbell (Australian politician)|Ian Campbell]].

''Feral Future: The Untold Story of Australia's Exotic Invaders'' (1999) surveyed the problems caused by invasive species. It was republished by the [[University of Chicago Press]]. An extract was read out in the Australian Senate. Low appeared in a TV New Zealand episode of ''Assignment'' named after the book. ''Feral Future'' inspired the formation of an NGO, the [[Invasive Species Council]].<ref>Faulkner, Jane; February 6, 2003; "Noxious Nasties"; The Age; newsstrore.fairfax.com.au.  Access date: November 17, 2016</ref> Low had spoken about its formation at the 18th Global Biodiversity Forum in Mexico in 2001.
 
His four earlier books helped popularise Australian bush tucker.<ref>Improving Access to Bushfood Production & Marketing Information Publication No. 99/158 (1999) Rural Industries Research and Development Corporation</ref> Four of his books have won national prizes.

He has written chapters and sections for many books.

==Bibliography==
* ''Wild Herbs of Australia and New Zealand'' (1985)
* ''Wild Food Plants of Australia'' (1989)
* ''Bush Tucker'' (1989)
* ''Bush Medicine'' (1990)
* ''Feral Future: The Untold Story of Australia's Exotic Invaders'' (1999)
* ''The New Nature: Winners & Losers in Wild Australia'' (2002)
* ''Where Song Began'' (2014)
